In enterprise Java testing with Mockito, writing clean unit tests requires orchestrating dependencies cleanly without manual object-graph instantiation. When testing service layers that depend on multiple repositories or clients, developers rely on Mockito annotations to automate test-double creation and wiring. Specifically, `@Mock`, `@InjectMocks`, and `@Spy` form the cornerstone of dependency management in test classes, each serving a fundamentally distinct purpose in how real or stubbed bytecode interacts under the hood.

The `@Mock` annotation creates a bare-metal mock of a specified class or interface. A mock has no real behavior by default; all non-void methods return default values (like null, 0, or false), and method invocations are intercepted by Mockito's invocation dispatcher rather than executing original code. The `@InjectMocks` annotation tackles the inverse problem: it instantiates the target class under test and attempts to inject all declared `@Mock` or `@Spy` fields into it via constructor injection, setter injection, or field reflection. Finally, the `@Spy` annotation wraps an existing real object. Unlike a mock, a spy executes real method logic when called unless explicitly stubbed using `doReturn().when()`, allowing developers to selectively mock specific behaviors of a concrete implementation while preserving the rest of its stateful execution.

items: @InjectMocks relies heavily on constructor injection first. If a matching constructor is found, Mockito passes the resolved mocks into it. If no suitable constructor exists, it falls back to setter injection and finally direct field reflection.

When using @Spy, calling `when(spyInstance.method()).thenReturn(value)` can occasionally throw an exception if the real method is executed during the stubbing phase before `when()` intercepts it; always use `doReturn(value).when(spyInstance).method()` instead.

Mockito annotations require initialization hooks to function. This is typically achieved by annotating the test class with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` in JUnit 5 or calling `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this)` in a `@BeforeEach` method.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production trap with @InjectMocks is assuming it performs deep or transitive dependency injection. Mockito only injects mocks into the immediate fields of the class annotated with @InjectMocks; it does not recursively wire mocks into dependencies of dependencies. If your service requires a collaborative tree, you must manually construct the sub-dependencies or refactor your design.
